summary.heading: Magnetic flux and flux linkage
summary.html:
$$\Phi = BA\cos\theta$$
  • Magnetic flux measures how much field passes through an area (like counting field lines). $\theta$ is the angle between the field and the normal to the area.
  • Unit: weber, $1\ \text{Wb} = 1\ \text{T m}^{2}$. Maximum when the field passes straight through ($\theta = 0$); zero when the field is parallel to the surface.
  • Flux linkage of a coil of $N$ turns: $N\Phi$.

summary.heading: Faraday's law
summary.html:
$$\varepsilon = -N\frac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$$
  • An emf is induced whenever the flux linking a circuit changes; the emf equals the rate of change of flux linkage. A steady flux, however large, induces nothing. A complete circuit carries an induced current.
  • The minus sign is Lenz's law.
  • Three ways to change $\Phi = BA\cos\theta$: change $B$ (move a magnet, switch a nearby current on or off); change $A$ in the field (move a coil in or out, slide a rod on rails); change $\theta$ (rotate a coil).
  • A faster change gives a bigger emf, even for the same total change of flux.
  • On a graph of flux linkage against time, the emf is minus the gradient: zero where the graph is flat, largest where it is steepest.

summary.heading: Moving conductors and coils
summary.html:
$$\varepsilon = BvL$$
  • For a straight conductor moving perpendicular to a uniform field: its free charges feel $qvB$ along it, and charge builds up until the electric force balances it. The same result follows from Faraday's law (the rod sweeps out area $Lv\Delta t$).
  • A rectangular coil at constant speed crossing a field region: entering, $\varepsilon = NBvL$ ($L$ = the leading edge); fully inside a uniform field, the flux is constant, so $\varepsilon = 0$; leaving, $\varepsilon = NBvL$ in the opposite direction.

summary.heading: Lenz's law and energy
summary.html:
• Lenz's law: the induced emf (and current) is in the direction that opposes the change that produced it.
  • N pole pushed towards a coil: the near end becomes N and repels it. Pulled away: the near end becomes S and attracts it back.
  • It is a consequence of energy conservation: if the induced current helped the change, energy would appear from nothing. The electrical energy produced comes from the work done against the opposing force.
  • Applications: electromagnetic braking (a magnet falling slowly down a copper pipe; braking of trains and roller coasters with no contact).

summary.heading: The ac generator
summary.html:
• A coil rotating steadily in a uniform field: $\theta = \omega t$ with $\omega = 2\pi f$, so the flux linkage varies sinusoidally and so does the emf (an alternating emf).
  • Plane of the coil perpendicular to the field: flux maximum, emf zero. Plane parallel to the field: flux zero, emf maximum. The emf is a quarter of a cycle out of step with the flux.
  • Doubling the rotation frequency doubles the peak emf and halves the period. The peak emf also rises with more turns, larger area or a stronger field.
  • Power stations run generators at constant speed to keep the mains frequency fixed (50 or 60 Hz).

summary.heading: Self-induction
summary.html:
• Changed for 2028 Qualitative only for exams before 2028; the 2028 guide no longer mentions it (inductance and RL circuits are not required either way).
  • A changing current in a coil changes the flux linking the coil itself, inducing an emf in the same coil. By Lenz's law this back emf opposes the change in current: it slows the rise at switch-on and tries to keep the current flowing at switch-off (sparks at switches).

summary.heading: Watch out for
summary.html:
• Thinking a large flux gives a large emf: only the rate of change of flux linkage matters.
  • Measuring $\theta$ in $\Phi = BA\cos\theta$ from the plane of the coil instead of the normal.
  • Forgetting $N$ in Faraday's law.
  • Saying a coil moving fully inside a uniform field has an emf.
  • Lenz direction: the induced current opposes the change in flux, not the flux itself.
  • Saying doubling a generator's frequency changes only the ac frequency: the peak emf doubles too.

Experiments: Faraday's meter flicked only at switch-on and switch-off. Why might other experimenters have missed this, or dismissed it as a fault?
Repeat the iron-ring experiment with two coils and a sensitive meter. Ask students to predict before switching on, while steady and at switch-off.
Patterns and trends: Ørsted showed currents make magnetic fields; Faraday looked for the reverse. Is searching for symmetry a good scientific strategy? Can students think of a case where it failed?
Why did it take eleven years to find induction, if people were looking for it?
Models: Faraday reasoned with field lines being 'cut'. Use the cutting picture and the changing-flux picture on the sliding rod: do they give the same answer?
Maxwell turned Faraday's pictures into equations. What did the equations add that the pictures could not?
Global impact: Almost all electricity comes from induction. List the energy sources that turn a generator and the few that don't (solar cells).
Who gained most, and who least, from large-scale electricity generation in the 1800s and today?

oracy.html:
Hot seat (whole class, 8 minutes): one student, the expert, answers the class's questions; swap experts every few questions. Situation: two light aluminium rings hang from threads, one complete, one cut through. A magnet pushed quickly towards each makes only the complete ring swing away. Why?

  • My question for the expert is …
  • Could you explain why …?
  • What would happen if …?

Listen for: the changing flux induces an emf in both rings, but current flows only in the complete one; by Lenz's law it opposes the change.

Does terminology help or hinder?: Ask students to explain the difference between flux, flux density and flux linkage in one sentence each. Where do they get stuck?
Should physics simplify its words for the public, or should the public learn the precise words?
Pictures or equations?: Faraday had little mathematics but made huge discoveries. Can visual reasoning ever be as rigorous as an equation?
Ask students whether they understand Lenz's law better from a picture of a magnet and coil, or from the minus sign in Faraday's law.
Is Lenz's law a law?: If Lenz's law follows from energy conservation, is it a separate law, or a consequence? Does the name matter?
Can students find another 'law' in physics that follows from a deeper principle?
Who benefits from discoveries?: When Faraday found induction, its uses were unknown. Should scientists be expected to predict the uses of their work?
Does a scientist share responsibility for harmful uses of a discovery, decades later?

videos.use: Filmed at the Royal Institution: a recreation of Faraday's 1831 coil-and-magnet experiment. A history hook for the Experiments NoS idea; ask students why the meter only moves while the magnet moves.
